title: When Pressure Drops, Contamination Moves Fast
excerpt: A negative pressure event in a distribution system is not just a loss of flow — it creates suction. EPA modeling found 69 to 78 gallons could intrude into a water line in under a minute. Backflow preventers are what stand between that event and your water supply.

heroFact.label: can intrude into a water line in 60 seconds
heroFact.context: EPA pilot-scale modeling of negative pressure events — pump-failure and main-break surges — showed 69 to 78 gallons of external water entering a distribution line within one minute.

title: A Backflow Device Isn't a Backflow Program
excerpt: Surveys cited by the EPA found many water storage facilities had never been inspected — and many more were inspected less often than AWWA's 3-year recommendation. A device on the wall is not the same as a program that keeps it working.

heroFact.label: is AWWA's maximum recommended inspection interval for water storage facilities
heroFact.context: EPA-cited surveys found many facilities were inspected less often than this — and many had never been inspected at all.

title: Why Pressure Loss Creates Backflow Risk: 11,186 Pressure-Reduction Incidents in One Year
excerpt: Backflow does not require a catastrophic failure. It requires only a pressure drop — and EPA-cited survey data shows those happen thousands of times a year, across ordinary systems, for entirely routine reasons.

title: Nearly One-Third of Community-Water Outbreaks Came From Distribution-System Contamination
excerpt: Treating water before it leaves the plant is only half the job. EPA data from nearly three decades shows that almost a third of all community-water outbreaks traced back to contamination that entered after the water was already clean.

title: The Backflow Problem We Probably Underreport: What EPA's Incident Gap Really Means
excerpt: EPA researchers cross-checked their backflow incident database against CDC outbreak records and found a striking gap: most illness events tied to backflow never made it into national surveillance summaries.

heroFact.label: backflow illness outbreaks that appeared in CDC national summaries
heroFact.context: EPA's incident database captured 75 outbreaks with illness data from 1981–1999. Only 26 showed up in CDC surveillance — fewer than 35% of known cases.

title: Backflow Isn’t Just Dirty Water: Biological vs. Chemical Contamination in the Outbreak Record
excerpt: Most people picture backflow as dirty water flowing the wrong way. The reality is more specific — and more useful. EPA records document two distinct contamination categories with different sources, different illness counts, and different prevention priorities.

heroFact.label: Traced to biological backflow outbreaks in U.S. community water systems, 1981–1998
heroFact.context: That figure comes from just 20 documented outbreaks — an average of over 300 people sickened per event. The EPA separates these from chemical contamination events, which produced a very different profile.
